keyPoints: ["The reference angle of an angle between 90 degrees and 180 degrees is 180 degrees minus the angle."]

i. $125^{\circ}$: reference angle $=180^{\circ}-125^{\circ}=55^{\circ}$

ii. $138^{\circ}$: reference angle $=180^{\circ}-138^{\circ}=42^{\circ}$

iii. $111^{\circ}$: reference angle $=180^{\circ}-111^{\circ}=69^{\circ}$

iv. $142^{\circ}$: reference angle $=180^{\circ}-142^{\circ}=38^{\circ}$
stem:
Find the reference angles of the following angles.
(i) $125^{\circ}$
(ii) $138^{\circ}$
(iii) $111^{\circ}$
(iv) $\quad 142^{\circ}$

keyPoints: ["Since sin(180 - theta) = sin(theta), the second-quadrant angle with the same sine as theta is 180 minus theta."]
modelAnswer:

$\theta=36^{\circ}\Rightarrow\alpha=180^{\circ}-36^{\circ}=144^{\circ}$
stem: If $\theta=36^{\circ}$. Find equivalent angle $\alpha$ in the second quadrant for which $\sin \alpha=\sin \theta$.

keyPoints: ["Since cos(180 - theta) = -cos(theta), the second-quadrant angle whose cosine is the negative of cos(theta) is 180 minus theta."]
modelAnswer:
$\cos(180^{\circ}-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, so if $\cos\beta=-\cos\theta$ and $\beta$ is in the second quadrant, then $\beta=180^{\circ}-\theta$.

$\theta=87^{\circ}\Rightarrow\beta=180^{\circ}-87^{\circ}=93^{\circ}$
stem: If $\theta=87^{\circ}$. Find equivalent angle $\beta$ in the second quadrant for which $\cos \beta=-\cos \theta$.

keyPoints: ["An angle in the second quadrant shares the same sine, cosine, and tangent magnitude as its reference angle (180 minus the angle), with cosine and tangent taking the negative sign there."]
modelAnswer:
Reference angle of $120^{\circ}$ is $180^{\circ}-120^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$.

$\sin120^{\circ}=\sin60^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$

$\cos120^{\circ}=-\cos60^{\circ}=-\dfrac12$

$\tan120^{\circ}=-\tan60^{\circ}=-\sqrt3$
stem: Using a reference angle, find the exact values of $\sin 120^{\circ}, \cos 120^{\circ}$ and $\tan 120^{\circ}$.

keyPoints: ["3-pi/4 radians is 135 degrees, a second-quadrant angle whose reference angle is pi/4 (45 degrees); the same sign rules (cosine and tangent negative, sine positive) apply as with degree measure."]
modelAnswer:
$\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=135^{\circ}$, reference angle $=180^{\circ}-135^{\circ}=45^{\circ}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

$\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$

$\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$

$\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-1$
stem: Using the reference angle, find $\cos \frac{3 \pi}{4}, \sin \frac{3 \pi}{4}$ and $\tan \frac{3 \pi}{4}$.

keyPoints: ["Once sin(theta) is recovered from cos(theta) via the Pythagorean identity, every ratio at (180 - theta) follows directly from cos(180-t) = -cos(t) and sin(180-t) = sin(t)."]
modelAnswer:
$\cos\theta=0.559\Rightarrow\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-0.559^2}=\sqrt{0.6875}\approx0.8292$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{0.8292}{0.559}\approx1.4834$.

v. $\sec(180^{\circ}-\theta)=\dfrac1{\cos(180^{\circ}-\theta)}\approx-1.789$

vi. $\operatorname{cosec}(180^{\circ}-\theta)=\dfrac1{\sin(180^{\circ}-\theta)}\approx1.206$

keyPoints: ["In a right triangle with the right angle at C, side a is opposite angle alpha and side b opposite angle beta; alpha + beta = 90 degrees, and the remaining sides follow from sin/cos/tan of whichever angle is known, or Pythagoras when two sides are known."]
modelAnswer:
Right triangle ABC, $\gamma=90^{\circ}$: $a$ is opposite $\alpha$, $b$ opposite $\beta$, $c$ is the hypotenuse, and $\alpha+\beta=90^{\circ}$.

i. $a=12,\beta=35^{\circ}$: $\alpha=55^{\circ}$. $b=a\tan\beta=12\tan35^{\circ}\approx8.40$ cm. $c=\dfrac{a}{\cos\beta}=\dfrac{12}{\cos35^{\circ}}\approx14.65$ cm

ii. $b=30,\alpha=25^{\circ}35'$ ($25.583^{\circ}$): $\beta=64.417^{\circ}$. $a=b\tan\alpha\approx30(0.4784)\approx14.35$ cm. $c=\dfrac{b}{\cos\alpha}\approx\dfrac{30}{0.9013}\approx33.29$ cm

iii. $a=50,b=25$: $c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{2500+625}=\sqrt{3125}\approx55.90$ cm. $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{a}{b}=2\Rightarrow\alpha\approx63.43^{\circ}$, $\beta\approx26.57^{\circ}$

iv. $a=30,c=40$: $b=\sqrt{c^2-a^2}=\sqrt{1600-900}=\sqrt{700}\approx26.46$ cm. $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{a}{c}=0.75\Rightarrow\alpha\approx48.59^{\circ}$, $\beta\approx41.41^{\circ}$

v. $a=24,\alpha=36^{\circ}15'$ ($36.25^{\circ}$): $\beta=53.75^{\circ}$. $c=\dfrac{a}{\sin\alpha}\approx\dfrac{24}{0.5920}\approx40.54$ cm. $b=\dfrac{a}{\tan\alpha}\approx\dfrac{24}{0.7332}\approx32.74$ cm

vi. $b=10,\alpha=70.5^{\circ}$: $\beta=19.5^{\circ}$. $a=b\tan\alpha=10\tan70.5^{\circ}\approx28.24$ cm. $c=\dfrac{b}{\sin\beta}\approx\dfrac{10}{0.3338}\approx29.96$ cm

keyPoints: ["Which area formula to use depends on what's given: two sides + included angle uses (1/2)bc sinA; two angles + one side uses (1/2)a^2 sinB sinC/sinA (with the third angle found from the angle sum); three sides uses Heron's formula.","A triangle only exists if the sum of any two sides exceeds the third (triangle inequality); sides 2, 2, 5 fail this and have no valid area."]
modelAnswer:
Using $\Delta=\tfrac12 bc\sin\alpha$ (two sides + included angle), $\Delta=\tfrac12 a^2\dfrac{\sin\beta\sin\gamma}{\sin\alpha}$ (two angles + one side), and Heron's formula $\Delta=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ (three sides), with angles converted from minutes as needed ($1^{\circ}=60'$):

i. $a=8,b=14,\gamma=68.7^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(8)(14)\sin68.7^{\circ}\approx56(0.9317)\approx52.2$ sq. units

ii. $b=30,c=25,\alpha=46^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(30)(25)\sin46^{\circ}\approx375(0.7193)\approx269.7$ sq. units

iii. $a=20,c=15,\beta=25^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(20)(15)\sin25^{\circ}\approx150(0.4226)\approx63.4$ sq. units

iv. $\beta=46^{\circ}50',a=43,c=52$ ($46^{\circ}50'=46.833^{\circ}$): $\Delta=\tfrac12(43)(52)\sin46.833^{\circ}\approx1118(0.7290)\approx815.1$ sq. units

v. $b=4.5,c=2.5,\alpha=65.2^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(4.5)(2.5)\sin65.2^{\circ}\approx5.625(0.9078)\approx5.11$ sq. units

vi. $a=2,b=2,c=5$: since $a+b=4<c=5$, these three lengths **do not satisfy the triangle inequality**, so no such triangle exists and no area can be computed here (this looks like a stem typo -- a valid triangle needs the sum of any two sides to exceed the third).

vii. $a=12,\alpha=44^{\circ},\beta=60^{\circ}$: $\gamma=180^{\circ}-44^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=76^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(12)^2\dfrac{\sin60^{\circ}\sin76^{\circ}}{\sin44^{\circ}}\approx72(1.2099)\approx87.1$ sq. units

viii. $b=30,\alpha=40^{\circ},\beta=80^{\circ}$: $\gamma=60^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(30)^2\dfrac{\sin40^{\circ}\sin60^{\circ}}{\sin80^{\circ}}\approx450(0.5653)\approx254.4$ sq. units

ix. $c=10,\alpha=75^{\circ},\beta=45^{\circ}$: $\gamma=60^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(10)^2\dfrac{\sin75^{\circ}\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin60^{\circ}}\approx50(0.7887)\approx39.4$ sq. units

x. $b=21,\beta=30^{\circ}15',\gamma=110^{\circ}$ ($\beta=30.25^{\circ}$): $\alpha=180^{\circ}-30.25^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=39.75^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(21)^2\dfrac{\sin39.75^{\circ}\sin110^{\circ}}{\sin30.25^{\circ}}\approx220.5(1.1909)\approx262.6$ sq. units

xi. $a=18.4,\alpha=65^{\circ}10',\beta=95.5^{\circ}$ ($\alpha=65.167^{\circ}$): $\gamma=180^{\circ}-65.167^{\circ}-95.5^{\circ}=19.333^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(18.4)^2\dfrac{\sin95.5^{\circ}\sin19.333^{\circ}}{\sin65.167^{\circ}}\approx169.28(0.3635)\approx61.5$ sq. units

xii. $c=25,\alpha=52.7^{\circ},\gamma=79^{\circ}24'$ ($\gamma=79.4^{\circ}$): $\beta=180^{\circ}-52.7^{\circ}-79.4^{\circ}=47.9^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(25)^2\dfrac{\sin52.7^{\circ}\sin47.9^{\circ}}{\sin79.4^{\circ}}\approx312.5(0.5995)\approx187.3$ sq. units

xiii. sides $18,21,32$: $S=35.5$. $\Delta=\sqrt{35.5(17.5)(14.5)(3.5)}=\sqrt{31528.4}\approx177.6$ sq. units

xiv. sides $20,26,37$: $S=41.5$. $\Delta=\sqrt{41.5(21.5)(15.5)(4.5)}=\sqrt{62234.4}\approx249.5$ sq. units

xv. sides $\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\tfrac14$: $S=\tfrac{13}{24}$. $\Delta=\sqrt{\tfrac{13}{24}\cdot\tfrac{1}{24}\cdot\tfrac{5}{24}\cdot\tfrac{7}{24}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{455}{331776}}\approx0.0370$ sq. units

xvi. sides $12.4,13.7,20.2$: $S=23.15$. $\Delta=\sqrt{23.15(10.75)(9.45)(2.95)}=\sqrt{6937.4}\approx83.3$ sq. units

xvii. sides $1.6,2.6,4.1$: $S=4.15$. $\Delta=\sqrt{4.15(2.55)(1.55)(0.05)}=\sqrt{0.8202}\approx0.906$ sq. units

keyPoints: ["Given two sides and the enclosed area, solving Delta = (1/2)(side1)(side2)sin(angle) for sin(angle) recovers the angle, remembering sine is positive for both an acute angle and its supplement."]
modelAnswer:
Triangle ABC with $\mathrm{AB}=15$, $\mathrm{BC}=8$, area $=40\,\mathrm{cm}^2$; AB and BC are the two sides meeting at $\angle B$.

a. $\Delta=\tfrac12(\mathrm{AB})(\mathrm{BC})\sin B\Rightarrow 40=\tfrac12(15)(8)\sin B=60\sin B\Rightarrow \sin B=\dfrac{40}{60}=\dfrac23\approx0.667$

b. $\angle B=\sin^{-1}(0.667)\approx41.8^{\circ}$ (or its supplement $\approx138.2^{\circ}$, since both an acute and an obtuse angle share the same sine; either gives a valid triangle with this area).

keyPoints: ["A parallelogram's area from two adjacent sides and the included angle is (side1)(side2)sin(angle); since sine peaks at 1, the area is greatest when that angle is 90 degrees (a rectangle)."]
modelAnswer:
a. A parallelogram is made of two congruent triangles each with sides $c,a$ and included angle $\theta$, each of area $\tfrac12 ca\sin\theta$, so the parallelogram's total area is:

$$\text{Area}=ac\sin\theta$$

b. Since $a$ and $c$ are fixed side lengths, the area is maximized when $\sin\theta$ is largest, i.e. $\sin\theta=1$, which happens at $\theta=90^{\circ}$.

keyPoints: ["A trapezoid's leg and base angle give its height via leg x sin(angle); the area is then (1/2)(sum of parallel sides)(height), the standard trapezoid area formula."]
modelAnswer:
Isosceles trapezoid, parallel sides 30 ft and 20 ft, legs 10 ft, base angle $60^{\circ}$.

Height $=$ leg $\times\sin60^{\circ}=10(0.8660)\approx8.660$ ft

Area $=\tfrac12(\text{sum of parallel sides})\times\text{height}=\tfrac12(30+20)(8.660)=25(8.660)\approx216.5$ sq. ft (exact value $125\sqrt3$)

stem: A garden is in the shape of an isosceles trapezoid. The lengths of the parallel sides of the garden are 30 feet and 20 feet, and the length of each of the other two sides is 10 feet. If a base angle of the trapezoid measures $60^{\circ}$, find the exact area of the garden.

keyPoints: ["Two triangles with equal corresponding side pairs have equal area whenever their included angles are supplementary, since sin(theta) = sin(180 - theta)."]
modelAnswer:
Area of $\triangle ABC=\tfrac12(\mathrm{AB})(\mathrm{BC})\sin B=\tfrac12(\mathrm{AB})(\mathrm{BC})\sin30^{\circ}$

Area of $\triangle DEF=\tfrac12(\mathrm{DE})(\mathrm{EF})\sin E=\tfrac12(\mathrm{AB})(\mathrm{BC})\sin150^{\circ}$ (using $\mathrm{DE}=\mathrm{AB}$, $\mathrm{EF}=\mathrm{BC}$)

Since $\sin150^{\circ}=\sin(180^{\circ}-150^{\circ})=\sin30^{\circ}$, both areas equal $\tfrac12(\mathrm{AB})(\mathrm{BC})(0.5)$, so the two triangles have **equal area**.

stem: In triangle $\mathrm{ABC}, \angle \mathrm{B}=30^{\circ}$ and in triangle $\mathrm{DEF}, \angle \mathrm{E}=150^{\circ}$. Show that if $\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{DE}$ and $\mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{EF}$, the areas of the two triangles are equal.

keyPoints: ["Given a triangle's area and two of its angles, the side opposite the (found) third angle can be recovered from the two-angles-one-side area formula solved for that side."]
modelAnswer:
Third angle $=180^{\circ}-40^{\circ}-65^{\circ}=75^{\circ}$.

The side whose length is wanted is the one between the two given $40^{\circ}$ and $65^{\circ}$ corners, i.e. the side opposite the $75^{\circ}$ angle. Using $\Delta=\tfrac12 a^2\dfrac{\sin\beta\sin\gamma}{\sin\alpha}$ with $\alpha=75^{\circ}$ (opposite $a$), $\beta=40^{\circ}$, $\gamma=65^{\circ}$:

$150=\tfrac12 a^2\dfrac{\sin40^{\circ}\sin65^{\circ}}{\sin75^{\circ}}\approx0.3016\,a^2\Rightarrow a^2\approx497.3\Rightarrow a\approx22.3$ m

keyPoints: ["A parallelogram's diagonal, its two adjacent sides, and the angle between them are related by the law of cosines, which recovers cos(theta) directly; sin(theta) then follows from the Pythagorean identity, and the area from side1*side2*sin(theta)."]
modelAnswer:
Parallelogram, adjacent sides $p=2$ km, $q=3$ km, shorter diagonal $d=3$ km, with $\theta$ the angle between the sides forming that diagonal.

By the law of cosines: $d^2=p^2+q^2-2pq\cos\theta\Rightarrow 9=4+9-12\cos\theta\Rightarrow12\cos\theta=4$

a. $\cos\theta=\dfrac13$

b. $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\tfrac19}=\sqrt{\tfrac89}=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$

c. Area $=pq\sin\theta=2\times3\times\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}=4\sqrt2$ km$^2$ (exact)

d. $4\sqrt2\approx5.657$, so to the nearest integer the area is **6 km$^2$**

keyPoints: ["Once the in-radius r = Delta/S is found from Heron's formula, the incircle's own area (pi r^2) and circumference (2 pi r) follow from the ordinary circle formulas."]
modelAnswer:
Sides $2.5,7.3,6.2$ cm: $S=\dfrac{2.5+7.3+6.2}{2}=8.0$

$\Delta=\sqrt{8(5.5)(0.7)(1.8)}=\sqrt{61.6}\approx7.85$

$r=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}=\dfrac{7.85}{8}\approx0.981$ cm

Area of in-circle $=\pi r^2\approx\pi(0.981)^2\approx3.02\,\mathrm{cm}^2$

Circumference of in-circle $=2\pi r\approx2\pi(0.981)\approx6.16$ cm
stem: Find the area and circumference of in-circle of a triangle having sides: $2.5 c m, 7.3 c m$ and 6.2 cm .

keyPoints: ["Substituting a = b = c into the general formulas for r, R, and the ex-radii reduces every one of them to a multiple of the single side length a, making their ratios purely numeric."]
modelAnswer:
For an equilateral triangle with side $a$: $S=\tfrac{3a}{2}$, $\Delta=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$.

$r=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}=\dfrac{\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2}{\tfrac{3a}{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{6}a$

$R=\dfrac{abc}{4\Delta}=\dfrac{a^3}{4\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2}=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}a$

$r_1=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}=\dfrac{\Delta}{a/2}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a$

i. $r:R:r_1=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{6}a:\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}a:\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a$. Multiplying every term by $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt3 a}$ gives $1:2:3$. **Proved.**

ii. Since the triangle is equilateral, $a=b=c$, so $S-a=S-b=S-c$, which makes $r_1=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}$, $r_2=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-b}$, $r_3=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-c}$ all equal. Hence $r_1:r_2:r_3=1:1:1$. **Proved.**
stem:
If ABC is an equilateral triangle, prove that:
(i) $\quad r: \mathrm{R}: r_{1}=1: 2: 3$
(ii) $r_{1}: r_{2}: r_{3}=1: 1: 1$

keyPoints: ["Which area formula to use depends on what's given: two sides + included angle uses (1/2)bc sinA; two angles + one side uses (1/2)a^2 sinB sinC/sinA (with the third angle found from the angle sum); three sides uses Heron's formula.","A triangle only exists if the sum of any two sides exceeds the third (triangle inequality); sides 2, 2, 5 fail this and have no valid area."]
modelAnswer:
Using $\Delta=\tfrac12 bc\sin\alpha$ (two sides + included angle), $\Delta=\tfrac12 a^2\dfrac{\sin\beta\sin\gamma}{\sin\alpha}$ (two angles + one side), and Heron's formula $\Delta=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$ (three sides), with angles converted from minutes as needed ($1^{\circ}=60'$):

i. $a=8,b=14,\gamma=68.7^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(8)(14)\sin68.7^{\circ}\approx56(0.9317)\approx52.2$ sq. units

ii. $b=30,c=25,\alpha=46^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(30)(25)\sin46^{\circ}\approx375(0.7193)\approx269.7$ sq. units

iii. $a=20,c=15,\beta=25^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(20)(15)\sin25^{\circ}\approx150(0.4226)\approx63.4$ sq. units

iv. $\beta=46^{\circ}50',a=43,c=52$ ($46^{\circ}50'=46.833^{\circ}$): $\Delta=\tfrac12(43)(52)\sin46.833^{\circ}\approx1118(0.7290)\approx815.1$ sq. units

v. $b=4.5,c=2.5,\alpha=65.2^{\circ}$: $\Delta=\tfrac12(4.5)(2.5)\sin65.2^{\circ}\approx5.625(0.9078)\approx5.11$ sq. units

vi. $a=2,b=2,c=5$: since $a+b=4<c=5$, these three lengths **do not satisfy the triangle inequality**, so no such triangle exists and no area can be computed here (this looks like a stem typo -- a valid triangle needs the sum of any two sides to exceed the third).

vii. $a=12,\alpha=44^{\circ},\beta=60^{\circ}$: $\gamma=180^{\circ}-44^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=76^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(12)^2\dfrac{\sin60^{\circ}\sin76^{\circ}}{\sin44^{\circ}}\approx72(1.2099)\approx87.1$ sq. units

viii. $b=30,\alpha=40^{\circ},\beta=80^{\circ}$: $\gamma=60^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(30)^2\dfrac{\sin40^{\circ}\sin60^{\circ}}{\sin80^{\circ}}\approx450(0.5653)\approx254.4$ sq. units

ix. $c=10,\alpha=75^{\circ},\beta=45^{\circ}$: $\gamma=60^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(10)^2\dfrac{\sin75^{\circ}\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin60^{\circ}}\approx50(0.7887)\approx39.4$ sq. units

x. $b=21,\beta=30^{\circ}15',\gamma=110^{\circ}$ ($\beta=30.25^{\circ}$): $\alpha=180^{\circ}-30.25^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=39.75^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(21)^2\dfrac{\sin39.75^{\circ}\sin110^{\circ}}{\sin30.25^{\circ}}\approx220.5(1.1909)\approx262.6$ sq. units

xi. $a=18.4,\alpha=65^{\circ}10',\beta=95.5^{\circ}$ ($\alpha=65.167^{\circ}$): $\gamma=180^{\circ}-65.167^{\circ}-95.5^{\circ}=19.333^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(18.4)^2\dfrac{\sin95.5^{\circ}\sin19.333^{\circ}}{\sin65.167^{\circ}}\approx169.28(0.3635)\approx61.5$ sq. units

xii. $c=25,\alpha=52.7^{\circ},\gamma=79^{\circ}24'$ ($\gamma=79.4^{\circ}$): $\beta=180^{\circ}-52.7^{\circ}-79.4^{\circ}=47.9^{\circ}$. $\Delta=\tfrac12(25)^2\dfrac{\sin52.7^{\circ}\sin47.9^{\circ}}{\sin79.4^{\circ}}\approx312.5(0.5995)\approx187.3$ sq. units

xiii. sides $18,21,32$: $S=35.5$. $\Delta=\sqrt{35.5(17.5)(14.5)(3.5)}=\sqrt{31528.4}\approx177.6$ sq. units

xiv. sides $20,26,37$: $S=41.5$. $\Delta=\sqrt{41.5(21.5)(15.5)(4.5)}=\sqrt{62234.4}\approx249.5$ sq. units

xv. sides $\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\tfrac14$: $S=\tfrac{13}{24}$. $\Delta=\sqrt{\tfrac{13}{24}\cdot\tfrac{1}{24}\cdot\tfrac{5}{24}\cdot\tfrac{7}{24}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{455}{331776}}\approx0.0370$ sq. units

xvi. sides $12.4,13.7,20.2$: $S=23.15$. $\Delta=\sqrt{23.15(10.75)(9.45)(2.95)}=\sqrt{6937.4}\approx83.3$ sq. units

xvii. sides $1.6,2.6,4.1$: $S=4.15$. $\Delta=\sqrt{4.15(2.55)(1.55)(0.05)}=\sqrt{0.8202}\approx0.906$ sq. units

modelAnswer:
Using $r=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}$, $R=\dfrac{abc}{4\Delta}$, $r_1=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}$, $r_2=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-b}$, $r_3=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-c}$, and $\Delta^2=S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)$:

i. $\dfrac1{ab}+\dfrac1{bc}+\dfrac1{ca}=\dfrac{c+a+b}{abc}=\dfrac{2S}{abc}$. Since $abc=4R\Delta$, this is $\dfrac{2S}{4R\Delta}=\dfrac{S}{2R\Delta}$; since $S=\Delta/r$, this becomes $\dfrac{\Delta/r}{2R\Delta}=\dfrac{1}{2rR}$. So $\dfrac1{ab}+\dfrac1{bc}+\dfrac1{ca}=\dfrac{2S}{abc}=\dfrac{1}{2rR}$.

ii. $\dfrac1{r_1}+\dfrac1{r_2}+\dfrac1{r_3}=\dfrac{(S-a)+(S-b)+(S-c)}{\Delta}=\dfrac{3S-2S}{\Delta}=\dfrac{S}{\Delta}$.

iii. $r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_1r_3=\Delta^2\left[\dfrac1{(S-a)(S-b)}+\dfrac1{(S-b)(S-c)}+\dfrac1{(S-a)(S-c)}\right]=\Delta^2\cdot\dfrac{(S-c)+(S-a)+(S-b)}{(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}=\Delta^2\cdot\dfrac{S}{\Delta^2/S}=S^2$.

iv. Using $r=4R\sin\tfrac{\alpha}2\sin\tfrac{\beta}2\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2$ and (by the same method as the note's worked $r_2$ example) $r_1=4R\sin\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$, $r_2=4R\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\sin\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$, $r_3=4R\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2$: summing $r_1+r_2+r_3-r$ gives $4R$ times a standard half-angle sum identity equal to $\sin\tfrac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}2=\sin90^{\circ}=1$ (since $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^{\circ}$). So $r_1+r_2+r_3-r=4R(1)=4R$. (Numeric check with $a=10,b=13,c=17$: $r_1+r_2+r_3-r\approx6.48+9.26+21.60-3.24=34.10\approx4R=4(8.53)$. Confirmed.)

v. $r\,r_1\,r_2\,r_3=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta}{S-b}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta}{S-c}=\dfrac{\Delta^4}{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}=\dfrac{\Delta^4}{\Delta^2}=\Delta^2$, so $\sqrt{r\,r_1\,r_2\,r_3}=\Delta$.

vi. $r_1r_2r_3=\dfrac{\Delta^3}{(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}=\dfrac{\Delta^3}{\Delta^2/S}=\Delta S=rS\cdot S=rS^2$.

keyPoints: ["Each side equals 2R times the sine of its opposite angle (law of sines rearranged); summing all three and dividing by 2R directly gives the sum of the sines in terms of S and R."]
modelAnswer:
By the law of sines, $a=2R\sin\alpha$, $b=2R\sin\beta$, $c=2R\sin\gamma$.

Adding: $a+b+c=2R(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)$

Since $a+b+c=2S$: $2S=2R(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)\Rightarrow\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma=\dfrac{S}{R}$
sectionLabel: Circum-Radius of Circle In-terms of Sides of Triangle
stem: Show that: $(\sin \alpha+\sin \beta+\sin \gamma)=\frac{S}{R}$

keyPoints: ["All three chained identities are proved the same way: substitute the half-angle sine/cosine/tangent formulas (built from S, S-a, S-b, S-c) and simplify using Delta^2 = S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c) until both sides collapse to Delta or r."]
modelAnswer:
Using the half-angle formulas $\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2=\sqrt{\tfrac{S(S-a)}{bc}}$ (and cyclic), $\Delta=\sqrt{S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}$, $R=\tfrac{abc}{4\Delta}$, $r=\tfrac{\Delta}S$:

i. $4rR\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$: the product of the three cosines works out to $\dfrac{S\Delta}{abc}$ (using the half-angle forms), so $4rR\times\dfrac{S\Delta}{abc}=4\cdot\tfrac{\Delta}S\cdot\tfrac{abc}{4\Delta}\cdot\dfrac{S\Delta}{abc}=\Delta$. Also $r^2\cot\tfrac{\alpha}2\cot\tfrac{\beta}2\cot\tfrac{\gamma}2=r^2/(r/S)=rS=\Delta$ (using that the product of the three tan-half-angles works out to $r/S$). So all three expressions equal $\Delta$.

ii. $r=4R\sin\tfrac{\alpha}2\sin\tfrac{\beta}2\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2$: the product of the three sines reduces, after substituting $R=abc/(4\Delta)$ and the half-angle sine forms, to exactly $\Delta/S=r$. Similarly $S\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2\tan\tfrac{\beta}2\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2=S\times(r/S)=r$.

iii. $r=a\sin\tfrac{\beta}2\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2\sec\tfrac{\alpha}2$: substituting the half-angle forms for $\sin\tfrac{\beta}2,\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2,\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2$ and simplifying gives $\sqrt{(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)/S}=\Delta/S=r$; the $b$- and $c$-versions follow identically by symmetry, so all three equal $r$.

keyPoints: ["An equilateral triangle's circumradius relates to its side by R = a/sqrt(3) (from R = a/(2 sin 60)); substituting back into the equilateral area formula (sqrt(3)/4)a^2 gives area purely in terms of R."]
modelAnswer:
For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius $R$, its side $a=R\sqrt3$ (from $R=\dfrac{a}{2\sin60^{\circ}}=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt3}$).

Area $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}(R\sqrt3)^2=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}(3R^2)=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}R^2$

With $R=6$ cm: Area $=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}(36)=27\sqrt3\approx46.77\,\mathrm{cm}^2$

keyPoints: ["Each ex-radius r_i = Delta/(S - side_i), where side_i is the side opposite that excircle; a smaller opposite side gives a smaller (S - side), hence a bigger ex-radius, and vice versa."]
modelAnswer:
Sides $5,9,10$: $S=\dfrac{5+9+10}{2}=12$. $\Delta=\sqrt{12(7)(3)(2)}=\sqrt{504}\approx22.45$

i. Ex-circle opposite the smaller side ($a=5$): $r_1=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}=\dfrac{22.45}{12-5}=\dfrac{22.45}{7}\approx3.21$

ii. Ex-circle opposite the larger side ($c=10$): $r_3=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-c}=\dfrac{22.45}{12-10}=\dfrac{22.45}{2}\approx11.22$

(Note: 'circumference' in the stem is used loosely for the ex-radius itself; if the actual circumference of that ex-circle is wanted, multiply each radius by $2\pi$: $\approx20.17$ and $\approx70.48$ respectively.)
sectionLabel: E-Radius of a Circle of a Triangle
stem:
The measures of sides of a triangle are $5 \mathrm{~cm}, 9 \mathrm{~cm}, 10 \mathrm{~cm}$. Find the circumference of ex-circle:
(i) opposite to smaller side
(ii) opposite to larger side

keyPoints: ["Both halves of the identity reduce to c once you substitute r_i = S tan(angle_i/2), r = (S - side)tan(angle/2), and the standard identity S = 4R cos(a/2)cos(b/2)cos(g/2)."]
modelAnswer:
Using the identities $r_1=S\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2$, $r_2=S\tan\tfrac{\beta}2$, $r_3=S\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$ and $r=(S-c)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$:

$(r_3-r)\cot\tfrac{\gamma}2=\left[S\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2-(S-c)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2\right]\cot\tfrac{\gamma}2=c\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2\cdot\cot\tfrac{\gamma}2=c$

For $(r_1+r_2)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$: since $\alpha+\beta=180^{\circ}-\gamma$, sum-to-product gives $\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2+\tan\tfrac{\beta}2=\dfrac{\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2}{\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2}$ (since $\sin\tfrac{\alpha+\beta}2=\sin(90^{\circ}-\tfrac{\gamma}2)=\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$). So:

$(r_1+r_2)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2=S\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2\cdot\dfrac{\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2}{\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2}=\dfrac{S\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2}{\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2}$

Using $S=4R\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$ (a standard identity following from $\Delta=4rR\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$ and $\Delta=rS$): this becomes $4R\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2\sin\tfrac{\gamma}2=2R\sin\gamma=c$ (law of sines).

So both $(r_1+r_2)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$ and $(r_3-r)\cot\tfrac{\gamma}2$ equal $c$. **Proved.**

stem: Prove that: $\left(r_{1}+r_{2}\right) \tan \frac{\gamma}{2}=\left(r_{3}-r\right) \cot \frac{\gamma}{2}=c$

keyPoints: ["r1 and r2 both follow the same derivation pattern as the textbook's own worked r2 example: substitute the half-angle formulas, simplify using Delta^2 = S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c), and the result collapses to Delta/(S - a) or Delta/(S - b)."]
modelAnswer:
Using half-angle formulas $\sin\tfrac{\alpha}2=\sqrt{\tfrac{(S-b)(S-c)}{bc}}$, $\cos\tfrac{\beta}2=\sqrt{\tfrac{S(S-b)}{ac}}$, $\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2=\sqrt{\tfrac{S(S-c)}{ab}}$ and $R=\tfrac{abc}{4\Delta}$:

i. $4R\sin\tfrac{\alpha}2\cos\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2$: the product of the three factors simplifies to $\dfrac{S(S-b)(S-c)}{abc}$, so $4R\times$ that $=4\cdot\tfrac{abc}{4\Delta}\cdot\dfrac{S(S-b)(S-c)}{abc}=\dfrac{S(S-b)(S-c)}{\Delta}$. Since $\Delta^2=S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)$, $S(S-b)(S-c)=\Delta^2/(S-a)$, so this becomes $\dfrac{\Delta^2/(S-a)}{\Delta}=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}=r_1$.

ii. By the same method with $\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta$ swapped, $4R\cos\tfrac{\alpha}2\sin\tfrac{\beta}2\cos\tfrac{\gamma}2=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-b}=r_2$ (this is exactly the worked example already established for $r_2$ in this chapter).

(ii) $\quad 4 R \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \sin \frac{\beta}{2} \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}=r_{2}$

keyPoints: ["Substituting the half-angle tangent formula into S*tan(angle/2) and simplifying with Delta^2 = S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c) collapses it to Delta/(S - side), i.e. the corresponding ex-radius."]
modelAnswer:
Using $r_1=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}$ and the half-angle formula $\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}$:

$S\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=S\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{S(S-b)(S-c)}{S-a}}$. Since $\Delta^2=S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)$, $S(S-b)(S-c)=\Delta^2/(S-a)$, giving $S\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=\sqrt{\dfrac{\Delta^2/(S-a)}{S-a}}=\dfrac{\Delta}{S-a}=r_1$. **Proved.**

By the identical argument with $b,\beta$ and $c,\gamma$ in place of $a,\alpha$: $r_2=S\tan\tfrac{\beta}2$ and $r_3=S\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$.
sectionLabel: E-Radius of a Circle of a Triangle
stem:
Prove that:
(i) $r_{1}=S \tan \frac{\alpha}{2}$
(ii) $r_{2}=S \tan \frac{\beta}{2}$
(iii) $r_{3}=S \tan \frac{\gamma}{2}$

keyPoints: ["Multiplying (S - side) by that side's half-angle tangent formula and simplifying with Delta^2 = S(S-a)(S-b)(S-c) always collapses to Delta/S, i.e. r, regardless of which side/angle pair is used."]
modelAnswer:
Using $r=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}$ and the half-angle formula $\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}$:

$(S-a)\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=(S-a)\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-a)^2(S-b)(S-c)}{S(S-a)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(S-a)(S-b)(S-c)}{S}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\Delta^2}{S^2}}=\dfrac{\Delta}{S}=r$

By the identical argument with $b,\beta$ and $c,\gamma$: $(S-b)\tan\tfrac{\beta}2=r$ and $(S-c)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2=r$. So $r=(S-a)\tan\tfrac{\alpha}2=(S-b)\tan\tfrac{\beta}2=(S-c)\tan\tfrac{\gamma}2$. **Proved.**
